title: Did medieval people love their children?  - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Philippe Ariès' influential 1960s claim that medieval parents saw children as defective adults and did not love them has been comprehensively refuted by later European scholarship, above all Nicholas Orme's Medieval Children. Medieval English households looked structurally similar to modern ones, parents spent roughly 15 percent of income feeding a child and generally received no economic return, and the closing lesson is to distrust scholarly claims that some class of human beings is incomprehensibly unlike us.

insights.claim: Philippe Ariès' 1960s argument that medieval childhood was profoundly remote, with children treated as defective or incomplete adults and not loved as parents love children today, never attained full academic acceptance but was vastly influential on the wider public.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A textbook case of an idea whose popular reach far exceeded its scholarly support, worth remembering whenever a striking historical claim circulates as common knowledge.
insights.locator: Growing up, I acquired a vague idea

insights.claim: A wealth of later scholarship across Europe has established beyond doubt that Ariès' view is untrue, and Nicholas Orme, whose Medieval Children is the leading study for England, writes that it is mistaken not simply in detail but in substance.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The consensus reversal is complete, so any model of pre-modern behavior built on emotional distance from children is starting from a falsified premise.
insights.quote: It cannot be overemphasised that there is nothing to be said for Ariès’s view

insights.claim: The medieval people who emerge from Orme's work are essentially recognizable as ourselves five hundred or a thousand years earlier, and it was never really plausible that children survived the hardship of medieval life without devoted parents.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A plausibility test worth applying to exotic behavioral claims: if the behavior would have prevented survival, it probably did not happen.
insights.quote: I believe they were ourselves, five hundred or a thousand years ago
insights.locator: The medieval people who emerge from Orme’s book

insights.claim: The general lesson is that when a scholar makes exciting claims that some class of human beings is incomprehensibly unlike us, the claim should be interrogated rather than accepted.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Directly applicable to behavioral and demographic forecasting, where models often assume other populations respond to incentives in fundamentally alien ways.
insights.quote: Next time a scholar makes exciting claims about how some class of human beings is incomprehensibly unlike us, we would do well to ask similar questions.
insights.locator: Perhaps we should ask why the Ariès hypothesis

insights.claim: Contrary to popular belief, most medieval people had only three or four children, somewhat more among the rich and fewer among the very poor, partly because in England they married quite late, generally in their mid or late twenties.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Pre-modern fertility in England was moderate and delayed by marriage age, undercutting narratives that treat high fertility as the natural pre-industrial default.
insights.locator: It is sometimes imagined that medieval people

insights.claim: About 25 percent of medieval English children died in their first year and another 15 percent by their tenth, yet the median English child grew up in a home with one sibling and two parents in their thirties or forties, exactly like the median English child today.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Household structure has been far more stable across a millennium than mortality rates suggest, which cautions against inferring social organization from demographic aggregates.
insights.locator: About 25 percent of children died in their first year

insights.claim: Surviving medieval grandparents often lived nearby but rarely under the same roof, so the multigenerational household was not the English norm.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Another point where the assumed pre-modern family archetype does not match the English evidence.

insights.claim: Medieval people believed early-term fetuses were alive but unconscious like vegetables and lacked souls, so early-term abortion was considered sinful but not homicide and was not punishable at common law, while late-term abortion was thought a kind of homicide yet also not normally punished at common law, a distinction that persisted until the nineteenth century.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Long-run legal history here is more gradated than modern debates assume, with sin and crime handled by separate institutions for centuries.

insights.claim: Feeding a single medieval child consumed about 15 percent of average income, and parents often continued supporting children throughout their adulthood.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A hard cost figure for pre-modern child-rearing that makes the observed family sizes look like deliberate, expensive choices rather than passive outcomes.

insights.claim: Children were usually sent away into apprenticeship or service at 13 or 14, precisely the age at which they might have become a net economic asset, and parents generally paid for the apprenticeship rather than receiving remittances, while grateful children supporting parents in old age does not appear to have been the norm.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the old-age-insurance model of pre-modern fertility, which matters for how economists explain fertility decline in developing economies today.
insights.locator: Older children often performed light work at home

insights.claim: Because medieval England was often at war and desperate for soldiers, the Crown repeatedly issued decrees banning "dishonest and useless" ballgames like football and requiring boys over the age of seven to practice archery instead, and the decrees were widely ignored.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: An early example of a state failing to redirect popular leisure toward strategically useful skills by decree, a limit on mobilization policy that still holds.
insights.locator: Medieval England was often at war

insights.claim: Few medieval diaries or letters survive in which parents expressed grief at child mortality, but it was sometimes recorded by others, as when the chronicler Matthew Parris wrote that Queen Eleanor of Provence fell sick with grief after the death of her disabled three-year-old daughter Katherine and could find no relief in medicine nor human consolation.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Absence of first-person emotional records is a source artifact rather than evidence of absent emotion, a general warning about inferring sentiment from surviving documents.
insights.quote: and could find no relief in medicine nor human consolation

insights.claim: Positive evidence of affection also survives: an Oxford schoolbook of the 1490s describes a schoolboy returning home for the holidays whose family wept for joy, and the thirteenth-century treatise Ancrene Wisse imagines Jesus playing hide-and-seek with a believer the way a mother plays with her child.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Devotional and pedagogical texts encode everyday emotional norms, making them a usable source class where personal records are missing.
insights.quote: we wept for joy, each to other
insights.locator: Parents also took joy in their children
